doc.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Career, market and the state of jazz
title: Generations in jazz: mentorship, David Murray and Wynton Marsalis's orchestra
summary: A possible disconnect between young and earlier generations, the basketball analogy and veterans in the Lincoln Center orchestra.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah I think that, I don’t think I’m the best person to answer that because I’m from San Francisco, I’m not part of like the New York scene. So in some ways it might come off kind of detached. But my initial feelings and it’s probably not even well thought out, is that David Murray is like, I think represents that last generation, the eighties. And I just remember one year when, I think it was 1990 or maybe it was the late eighties, there was a young saxophonist, Christopher Holliday, and he was sort of — maybe Jackie McLean, I don’t know if he was a mentor or a clone — but here’s a young kid that the music industry — I shouldn’t say young kid, he was a young adult — that the music industry chose to record and here’s Clifford Jordan who hadn’t had a recording date. So he’s like a generation, maybe one or two generations, I can’t even think of what the age difference with David Murray, and I always found that David Murray connected with so many

musicians like I sat in his big band one time and they had Sunny Murray and it was a great, great experience with Butch Morris doing conduction. And so he has these ties. But I don’t know if there is that kind of mentor relationship now.
Well we certainly have the universities to teach jazz. Maybe the mentor thing has been replaced by that, by all the programs.

Well it’s kind of like I use the analogy of a basketball team. If you have a veteran team, and now this is before they’ve even played a game, but like the Los Angeles Lakers, they’re champions because they have veterans and young players. Now they have a 40- year-old, Malone, they’ve got 35-year-old Payton, a 30-year-old Shaquille O’Neall, 25- year-old Kobe Bryant. I mean of course they’re Hall of Famers so you can’t really use the age as a factor, you have to factor in that variable. But you have veterans and young players. If you just have young players then you’ve got the Los Angeles Clippers. So see I’m trying to recall like I don’t know the full story about that but I heard that Wynton Marsalis had like older musicians in the Lincoln Jazz Center Orchestra. I think — was Roland Hanna — anyway he had older musicians and then I heard all of a sudden they were gone and he just had musicians that were, I don’t know 35 or 30 and younger. And so I thought that was a loss for Wynton’s jazz orchestra. Because that could have been a very beneficial experience for both the older musicians and the younger musicians.
